Site conditions—Amenities for older people in Sacramento and children in Seattle are described on page 19. Children and old people are found in most communities, yet there is no mention that these groups receive specific consideration in other areas. Are different sites being designed or slanted toward different groups? Considerable thought has been given to designing communities in urban areas to cater to different groups based on the services offered and the costs of living there. People would have a choice based on their preferred life style versus how much they were willing (or able) to pay.
On the same page it is noted that progressive approaches to minimize environmental degradation are being taken at two locations. Hopefully, these approaches are being taken at all sites, and the following paragraphs indicate this to be the case. However, the statement is misleading as written and should be clarified or omitted.
Social implications--Cluster development is emphasized in Operation Breakthrough. Massive multistory housing may be one means of solving immediate housing needs, but social and psychological implications arising from too close living should be taken into consideration. The benefits from a well-planned mass housing program--such as schools and retention of recreational areas--could be undone by social reaction. Although the prototype sites selected are well planned, and they probably will demonstrate the feasibility of systems building, a followup program should be incorporated. Under the control of your Department, environmental aspects have been considered. What will happen, however, if future projects are left in the hands of private developers?
Mineral resources—Operation Breakthrough, in the experimental stages, poses no current problems relating directly to the mineral industries. The ultimate effects, however, are likely to be numerous. Site selection will have to be studied on a case basis to assess possible land use conflicts. The operations producing construction minerals—the very minerals upon which this project depends—should not be zoned out of access or covered by physical structures before the minerals are extracted.
The minerals industries will be greatly affected if this program supplies the impetus to expand construction activities. Construction is the principal or a major market for asphalt, concrete, glass, gypsum, plastics, steel, aluminum and copper. The resources for most of the mineral raw materials are adequate for the near future, but further development of these operations must be consistent with ecological and environmental standards.
